newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU meets to discuss Irish plan to ease fish cuts.
newsitem.headline: EU meets to discuss Irish plan to ease fish cuts.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers met on Friday for tough talks on an Irish compromise watering down proposals for sharp cuts in fish catches.
Ireland, the current EU president, this week suggested a 20 percent cut over three years for the most threatened stocks and greater flexibility to member states over how to reduce fishing.
"The compromise proposal gives choice to people. They can either reduce activity or reduce capacity," Irish Marine Minister Sean Barrett told reporters before the meeting.

The European Commission, warning that drastic action was needed to save stocks, proposed in May cuts, mainly in capacity, of up to 40 percent over six years for boats hunting the worst affected species, such as North Sea cod and herring.
Barrett agreed that action was needed, warning, "Unless there are changes some stocks are going to disappear."
But little progress was expected on Friday.

British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry reiterated that Britain would not implement any further major cuts until the problem of "quota hoppers" -- boats from one EU state which register in another to take part of its quota -- is resolved.
The issue was being dealt with by an intergovernmeantal conference on the future of the EU, which is only expected to end next summer.

"It's a crazy situation where some 20 percent of the UK fleet is now effectively foreign owned, controlled, skippered, crewed...bringing no economic benefit to the fishing communities of the UK," Baldry told reporters as he entered the meeting.
Baldry said the new Irish text needed more study.

"It's a very complex compromise and I shall be very surprised if we make very much progress on it today," he said, adding he was concerned that it did very little to curb large scale industrial fishing.
But Portugal said the Irish initiative was acceptable.

"It's a good proposal," Portuguese Fisheries Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva told reporters, adding that only aid for fishermen leaving the industry and rules for small coastal vessels needed improvement.
But Portugal, like others, is against further fleet cuts.
Portugal argues it was the only country, along with Spain and Denmark, to meet capacity reduction targets set in the 1992-96 EU programme.

Some officials said that given continued strong opposition from mainly northern fishing member states, the current five-year programme, which expires at the end of December, could be extended for another year.
The EU's executive Commission has warned that any delay would be irresponsible as it would threaten the long-term survivial of the European fishing industry.
Ministers spent the morning session discussing a proposal to set up a satellite system for monitoring fishing vessels and were only due to examine the Irish compromise in the afternoon.
